We are a team of tech enthusiasts interested in AI/ML, software development, problem-solving, and space exploration. We enjoy learning new technologies and building creative solutions to real-world challenges.

Our team brings together curiosity, technical skills, and a passion for innovation. We are excited to explore NASA's open data and build something impactful! 🚀
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive mission planning workstation (built by Team Beyond404) which assists the planner in determining where and when a spacecraft can land and survive in the vicinity of the Moon’s south pole.

The South Pole is one of the most difficult places to land. The Sun is only 1.5 to 3 degrees above the horizon in some areas, there are deep craters that never see the Sun, the Earth is out of line-of-sight behind ridges and long polar nights will of course drain the batteries. Our app takes all of that and turns it into clear, hard numbers. It uses the NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris (which we've checked is to within 0.008 degrees), the LRO LOLA topography and the Diviner thermal data to work out the real time Sun and Earth geometry, the direct to Earth communication windows and the proximity to permanently shadowed regions for 2027/2028.

Users can explore sites in 3D orbital view, walk the surface at eye level with a shadow ruler and a slope hazard map, run a battery survival simulator and rank launch windows using a 4 factor suitability score (Solar, Night, Comms, Slope). Side by side comparison and printable reports are available to support real decisions.

It's important because bad site and bad timing can kill a mission. Lunar Navigator enables that analysis to be done quickly for everyone from agencies right through to students, helping to ensure safer Artemis and commercial lunar landings.
https://github.com/pavan-pks/lunar-navigator
details:
What it does and how it works

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser-based mission-planning workstation for evaluating lunar south-pole landing sites across the 2027 to 2028 epochs. The user picks a site (Shackleton, Malapert, Haworth, Connecting Ridge, Nobile, Chandrayaan-3’s Shiv Shakti Point, or any custom coordinates), sets a launch date, transit time, and slip, and the app instantly recomputes the Sun and Earth geometry for that landing time.

  • Ephemeris: Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL Horizons (DE440), verified to under 0.008° across 18 landing coordinates.
  • Horizon masks: Crater-rim elevation profiles from LRO LOLA terrain model ridges that block the low Sun and the Earth link.
  • Suitability score (0 to 100): Solar illumination 35%, Night survival 25%, Earth comms 25%, Slope safety 15%.
  • Battery simulator: Answers “Will the lander survive the night?” by comparing a deck-mounted panel with a vertical sun-tracking mast, which captures over 28 times more power at grazing angles.
  • Opportunity calendar: A full-year heatmap of 23 sites showing the best landing windows at a glance.
  • Surface view: A human-eye-level walk (1.7 m) on a 400 m patch, with a shadow ruler and a slope-hazard map (under 6° safe, 6° to 15° caution, over 15° hazard).
  • Extras: Delta-v trajectory budget, side-by-side site comparison, and printable mission reports.

Benefits and intended impact

Planners get objective, repeatable answers in seconds instead of relying on judgment, with no install needed. We want to make early lunar mission analysis accessible to agencies, commercial lander teams, students, and educators, and to help reduce risk for safer Artemis-era landings.

Tools used

React 19, Vite, Three.js with React Three Fiber, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Recharts, and Vitest (41 unit tests). Hosted on Vercel. It runs in any WebGL 2.0 browser, with no special hardware.

NASA data used

JPL Horizons, LRO LOLA and LROC QuickMap, LRO Diviner thermal data, NASA Artemis and CLPS site coordinates, and ISRO Chandrayaan-3.

Creativity

It connects orbital and ground-level views in one tool, turns the survival question into an interactive simulation, and uses a clean instrument-style interface. Shareable URL links let a team send an exact scenario.

Factors considered

We prioritized scientific honesty. The app states its limits openly: distant terrain is approximated by a horizon mask, the surface patch is procedural, Earth visibility is geocenter-based, light-travel delay is ignored, and dates outside 2027 to 2028 trigger a warning. We also focused on accuracy testing and on clear, color-coded verdicts for non-experts.

Source code (MIT licensed): https://github.com/pavan-pks/lunar-navigator
